units.translation: 429 ff. In the oldest legal procedure, which the Eumenides alone know, there was no other means of proof than the oath of the parties; see the classic passage on this in ⟦1⟧: ⟦2⟧ — — ⟦3⟧. Plato argues with some irony that this was appropriate at that time, because all people still believed firmly in gods, but is no longer appropriate today because of unbelief and perjury; therefore one must abolish the oath of the interested parties and have only the disinterested judges swear. Aeschylus, who in this very play shows himself to be a political and also juristic thinker, is evidently of the same opinion; for while Attic law did not decide according to the oath of the parties, but still inconsistently demanded this oath (the ⟦4⟧, ⟦5⟧, ⟦6⟧) in blood courts and elsewhere (⟦7⟧), Aeschylus in the archetypal blood-court procedure presented here simply omits the ⟦8⟧, whereas the judges are also sworn in his account. Cf. below on 485 f. Thus Athena also gives as her reason for rejecting the old procedure at v. 432: ⟦9⟧ (⟦10⟧) ⟦11⟧. —
of Rhadamanthys, in the so-called judgment of lawsuits, it is worth admiring
for by giving an oath to the disputants about each of the matters in dispute, he settled them quickly and safely
by oaths the things that are not
I say that unjust things should not prevail
At v. 429 in any case ⟦1⟧ is to be written instead of ⟦2⟧, since this fact cannot yet have been established, but otherwise nothing is to be changed.

At v. 430 in M ⟦1⟧. ⟦2⟧ (but ov on an erasure) and as a transmitted variant ⟦3⟧ (so fg) are preserved; Dindorf writes ⟦4⟧, from which he supplements ⟦5⟧ to ⟦6⟧: "You prefer to be called just rather than to act justly." The reproach would not exactly be deserved, and the parallel verse ⟦7⟧ (⟦8⟧) ⟦9⟧ (cf. also ⟦10⟧ ⟦11⟧) leads in a quite different direction: the emphasis must lie on ⟦12⟧, as there on ⟦13⟧. Thus as a question (as the scholiast also understands it, whose explanation is, moreover, useless): do you prefer to be called just or to achieve your purpose, better "to carry out the vengeance" (624)? Or, since thus ⟦14⟧ must be rendered with "or", differently from the parallel passages, where it is "than" and attaches to ⟦15⟧, with the slight change of ⟦16⟧ into
to be called cowardly rather than bloodthirsty
I wish to be ignorant rather than wise in evils
